name: Third-Person Effect
description: People tend to think persuasive or harmful media messages affect other people more than themselves. We imagine ourselves as relatively immune while assuming others are easier to sway.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to misinformation warnings, ad disclosures, political content UX, safety messaging, and persuasive product copy. Teams and users may assume the risky influence is mainly a problem for 'other people,' which changes how interventions are framed.
prevalence_note: Well established in communication, media, and persuasion research, and occasionally useful in trust-and-safety or civic-information product work, but not common everyday design-practice vocabulary.

findings.description: A meta-analysis of the perceptual component of the third-person effect covering 60 papers, 106 studies, and 372 effect sizes found that third-person perception is robust and not just a methodological artifact: people consistently judge media messages as influencing others more than themselves. The strength of the effect varies with message desirability, perceived vulnerability/similarity of the 'others,' and whether those others are likely audience members.
findings.source_title: Understanding the Third-Person Perception: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis
